breakdown.understanding:
I read the epic against the tree as it stands after #15 merged (97938bb) and checked each of the nine findings rather than trusting the report. All nine still reproduce: the guard at server/schedules/app.ts:589 still has no `.options`, the `unpaidDates` filter at shared/schedules.ts:596 still runs per date, Balance.tsx:103 still parses by hand, both schedule release notes are still in upcoming-release-notes/, useSchedules.ts:147-169 still resets both maps to empty, app.ts:233-244 is still the flattened ternary, transactions.test.ts still carries the parsePreviewId describe, Account.tsx:1571-1583 still drops the parsed date on both the today and the skip branch, and postTransactionForSchedule still stamps `next_date` on the today path. There is no spec on this branch (no docs/trd.md, no .sdlc/memory/spec-index.json), so nothing here carries a Covers line and the epic closes on its children alone.

What is left after splitting: four behaviour defects and one housekeeping ticket. The behaviour defects are four different user promises — an occurrence is written once, an action hits the row you clicked, an unpaid occurrence stays listed, and the list does not blink on refresh — and none of them is a prerequisite for another. Ordering is by risk, not by dependency: the double-write first because it is money and it is a one-line query option that should not wait behind anything, then the actions, then the two preview-list defects, then the housekeeping. The two preview defects are ordered with the refresh tear *before* the matching fix on purpose: the tear makes rows disappear for a round trip, and leaving it in place while QA exercises the matching fix would produce exactly the symptom QA is trying to attribute.

**Clubbing test, every adjacent pair.**

*R1 (duplicate guard) vs Q1+Q2 (actions act on the selected row)* — highest overlap of anything here: R1 is a query option on `postTransactionForSchedule`, the same function Q1's fix rewrites, and together they are three small changes and would fit one PR. Two of three answers point at clubbing and I am splitting anyway, so here is the reasoning rather than a shrug. Standalone value is high for both and the two are separately demonstrable: R1's repro is post an occurrence, split the transaction, dispatch the same occurrence again; Q1/Q2's repro is click a later Upcoming row and watch a different occurrence change. What decides it is sequencing risk — R1 is a one-line, provably-safe widening that can ship today, while Q1/Q2 need a real decision about what "Post transaction today" means for the earlier occurrence, and a decision like that can sit at a human gate for a while. A one-line money guard should not be parked behind a semantics discussion. A reviewer who thinks the two belong in one PR has the better argument on file-surface grounds and should say so.

*Q1+Q2 vs R2 (preview matching)* — no file overlap at all (Account.tsx and app.ts against shared/schedules.ts), independent triggers, and both independently demoable. Split.

*Q1+Q2 vs R5 (refresh tear)* — no overlap (post/skip paths against the useSchedules hook), and neither can be built only after the other. Split.

*R2 (preview matching) vs R5 (refresh tear)* — this is the pair that looks like a split and isn't. Both present as "my Upcoming rows disappeared", which invites clubbing. But they share no file, share no cause and share no fix: R5 is the hook resetting `statuses` and `postedTransactionsBySchedule` to empty and publishing on whichever of two queries returns first; R2 is the 2-day unstamped fallback matching one transaction against three consecutive occurrences. Each is a separate one-line-to-one-function fix with its own QA script, and coupling them would make a revert of one take out the other. Split, and put the tear first for QA clarity as described above.

*R5 vs R3+R4+R6 (housekeeping)* — obviously split: one is a user-visible regression in the register, the other changes no behaviour at all. Putting a chore in a bug PR is the thing the vertical-slice rule exists to prevent.

**Clubbed, deliberately.** *Q1 and Q2 into one piece:* the epic says itself that the skip fix is "the same fix shape" as the post-today fix, both live in the same `onScheduleAction` switch that already parses the preview id and discards the date on two branches, and together they are two source files. One work order. *R3, R4 and R6 into one piece:* three review leftovers with no user-visible behaviour between them — one unmigrated call site whose two forms the epic confirms are equivalent, one duplicate release note, one pure re-indentation revert — 3 files, roughly 30 lines, nothing a browser can show, and each alone would pay a full plan/implement/review/QA cycle for a line or two. One chore.

**Dropped.** R7 — the tests added outside the work order's `tests[]`. Its own finding says the tests are correct and would pass, and the only action offered was to drop the describe or amend a work order that no longer exists; the tests are now the coverage for a function six call sites depend on. There is nothing here to build, so filing it would be filing a non-issue.

pieces.title: A posted occurrence is never posted twice, even after its transaction is split
pieces.why: Posting the same occurrence of a schedule twice — after its transaction has been split, or after a menu item is double-clicked — creates exactly one transaction, so a schedule can no longer be paid twice for one occurrence.
pieces.context:
Two surfaces, one file. What a person sees: selecting an Upcoming row in an account register and choosing Post transaction never produces a second transaction for an occurrence they have already paid for. What the contract is: the duplicate-occurrence guard in `postTransactionForSchedule` (packages/loot-core/src/server/schedules/app.ts:585-597), which queries `q('transactions').filter({ schedule, schedule_occurrence })` with no `.options({ splits: 'all' })`, so AQL defaults to `inline` and appends `is_parent = 0`. `getHasTransactionsQuery` and `getPostedScheduleTransactionsQuery` in shared/schedules.ts both pass `splits: 'all'`, so today the guard and the status query disagree about whether a split parent's stamp exists. `splitTransaction` (shared/transactions.ts:362-391) keeps the original row as the parent with `is_parent: true`, and `makeChild` copies neither `schedule` nor `schedule_occurrence`, so the stamp survives only on the row the guard excludes.

Fix as the epic states it: add `.options({ splits: 'all' })` so the guard matches the same rows the other two queries match. A broader guard can only ever see more rows, never fewer. The QA script is: post an occurrence from the register, split that transaction, dispatch `schedule/post-transaction` again for the same schedule id and occurrence date, and observe one transaction, not two.
acceptance: Posting a schedule occurrence, splitting the resulting transaction, and dispatching the same occurrence again leaves exactly one transaction for that occurrence
The duplicate-occurrence guard in postTransactionForSchedule matches the same rows getHasTransactionsQuery and getPostedScheduleTransactionsQuery match, including a split parent carrying the stamp
An existing test covers post-then-split-then-post for the same occurrence, and the full loot-core schedules test suite still passes
pieces.risk: Money. This is the guard that decides whether one occurrence can be paid twice, and it is a widening of a query's row set on the write path. The direction is safe — a broader guard sees more rows and never fewer — but it can make an occurrence that a user genuinely still owes read as already posted, so the test must cover the split-parent case and not only the duplicate case.

pieces.title: Schedule actions from an upcoming row affect the occurrence you clicked
pieces.why: Choosing Post transaction today or Skip next scheduled date on a later Upcoming row changes only that row: the earlier occurrence you are still owed stays listed and stays payable, and the one you picked is the one that is posted or skipped.
pieces.context:
Two surfaces, two files. What a person sees: in an account register, select the 10/17 Upcoming row of a weekly schedule and choose Skip next scheduled date — 10/17 leaves the list, 10/03 (still owed) stays. Select the same row and choose Post transaction today — one transaction dated today appears, 10/17 is consumed, 10/03 is untouched. At present both actions operate on `next_date` and silently consume 10/03. What the contract is: `onScheduleAction` in packages/desktop-client/src/components/accounts/Account.tsx:1558-1594 already parses every preview id into `{ scheduleId, date }` via `parsePreviewId`, then discards the date on the `post-transaction-today` and `skip` branches — the `post-transaction` branch is the one PR #15 threaded it through. On the server, `postTransactionForSchedule` (app.ts:565-610) sets `const occurrence = today ? schedule.next_date : (date ?? schedule.next_date)` and keeps the deliberate comment that `today` pays `next_date` early; `skipNextDate` (app.ts:466-467) calls `setNextDate({ id, advance: true })` unconditionally, which is why selecting a later row skips the earliest.

Two shapes are available and the piece must pick one and say which: thread the parsed date through both handlers so the action names the occurrence (the shape the epic calls out as identical for both), or make the preview's `status === 'paid'` shift account for which occurrence was actually paid. The first is what the epic recommends and what the `post-transaction` branch already does. Whichever is chosen, the fix lands in the same `onScheduleAction` switch — this is one issue, not two, because the two branches are the same defect and the same switch.
acceptance: On a weekly schedule with 1 month of upcoming length, choosing Skip next scheduled date from the 10/17 Upcoming row removes 10/17 from the register and leaves 10/03 and 10/10 listed
On the same schedule, choosing Post transaction today from the 10/17 Upcoming row creates one transaction dated today, consumes 10/17, and leaves 10/03 listed as still payable
Both actions still work unchanged when the row selected is next_date itself, which is the case they get right at present
The existing tests for the post-transaction branch and for schedule preview computation still pass
pieces.risk: Money and date arithmetic. This changes what next_date means for two user-facing actions and which occurrence a written transaction is stamped with. Stamping the wrong occurrence un-pays an occurrence the user already paid; skipping the wrong occurrence silently drops money they were owed. The three pre-existing release notes for scheduled-transaction posting describe behaviour this change must not contradict — re-read them before deciding the fix shape.

pieces.title: Upcoming rows stop disappearing when schedule data refreshes
pieces.why: Editing a schedule, or any sync event that touches it, no longer blanks the Upcoming rows out of the register for a round trip — the scheduled rows stay on screen until their new data arrives.
pieces.context:
Two surfaces, one file. What a person sees: with a schedule selected in an account register showing Upcoming rows, edit the schedule or let a sync land; the Upcoming rows stay. At present they vanish for the duration of one query round trip and then reappear. What the contract is: `useSchedules` (packages/desktop-client/src/hooks/useSchedules.ts:135-190). Its `onData` fires again on every schedules change, unsubscribes the two dependent queries, then declares `let statuses: ScheduleStatuses = new Map()` and `let postedTransactionsBySchedule = new Map()`, opens both `loadStatuses` and `loadPostedTransactions` synchronously, and calls `publish()` from whichever returns first. The posted-transactions query is a plain `$or` selecting three columns; the status query is an `$or` of per-schedule `$and` branches with a `calculate` upstream. The cheaper query is expected to win, so the tear is the common case rather than the rare one. `setIsLoading(true)` lives in the effect body keyed on `[query, upcomingLength]` and never in `onData`, so the initial mount is masked (gated behind `isSchedulesLoading` in usePreviewTransactions.ts:77-79) while a refresh is not: `isForPreview` rejects every schedule on an empty status map, `schedulesForPreview` comes back empty, and Balance.tsx:92-95 gates only on `isLoading`.

Fix as the epic states it: do not reset the two maps to empty on refresh — seed them from the currently published data before re-opening the queries. That is the smaller change and it also stops `statusLabels` being rebuilt on every posted-transaction event. packages/desktop-client/src/hooks/useSchedules.test.ts exists and is the place this is proven.
acceptance: With Upcoming rows showing in an account register, a schedules-table refresh (a schedule edit or a sync event touching schedules) leaves those rows on screen without a gap
The register shows Upcoming rows once the schedules query returns, rather than waiting for the slower status query
A test drives useSchedules through two onData cycles where the posted-transactions query resolves first, and the published data never pairs a schedule list with an empty status map
The existing useSchedules and usePreviewTransactions tests still pass

pieces.title: A schedule's unpaid occurrences all stay listed when occurrences are close together
pieces.why: On a schedule whose occurrences are a day or two apart, one linked transaction stops at most one Upcoming row instead of silently removing three, so a payment that discharges one occurrence leaves the others visible.
pieces.context:
Two surfaces, one file. What a person sees: on a daily or every-other-day schedule in the register, one schedule-linked transaction removes exactly the one Upcoming row it paid and leaves the rest. At present it can remove three consecutive Upcoming rows. What the contract is: `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` (packages/loot-core/src/shared/schedules.ts:594-604) applies `isScheduleOccurrencePosted` to every date in the occurrence window. For a UI-created recurring schedule the date condition is `isapprox` and `posts_transaction` is false, so `getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate` returns occurrenceDate minus 2 days for exactly the schedule kind users create by hand (desktop-client/src/components/schedules/schedule-edit-utils.ts:49 and ScheduleEditModal.tsx:76), and `isScheduleOccurrencePosted`'s fallback arm accepts any transaction dated between that bound and the occurrence date. One-day-apart occurrences are reachable — RecurringSchedulePicker.tsx:40 offers 'Days'. Unstamped schedule-linked transactions are the norm, not a rarity: server/rules/action.ts:235-236 (`link-schedule`) never sets `schedule_occurrence`, so every rule-matched transaction on a synced budget takes the fallback arm. Before #15 only `next_date` was ever tested, so at most the head could be dropped; #15 widened it to every date in the window.

Fix as the epic states it: narrow the fallback so one transaction discharges at most one occurrence — for example, match each transaction to the earliest still-unmatched occurrence rather than testing each occurrence against every transaction — or leave multi-day-lookback matching to the status query alone. Read the comment block at shared/schedules.ts:584-593 first: the `status === 'paid'` shift and the `unpaidDates` filter are deliberately not redundant, and a narrowing must keep them that way.
acceptance: On a schedule with occurrences one day apart, a single unstamped schedule-linked transaction removes exactly one Upcoming row, and the other Upcoming rows for that schedule remain listed
An unstamped transaction dated up to two days before an occurrence still discharges that occurrence, so the early-payment fallback keeps working
A schedule whose date condition is an exact 'is' match, or which posts transactions automatically, behaves as it does now
shared/schedules.ts tests cover a multi-day lookback window and pass
pieces.risk: This narrows what counts as paid, on the preview path that decides which rows a user can still pay. A narrowing that is too aggressive re-offers an occurrence they already paid and risks a double payment; one that is too loose is the current defect. Note the dependency in the other direction: the refresh tear above makes rows disappear for a round trip, so ship that first or QA will see its symptom here.

pieces.title: Housekeeping from the schedule-occurrence PR: preview id parse, duplicate release note, setNextDate shape
pieces.why: Nothing a user can see changes; what changes is that the schedule code reads the way the rest of the codebase reads, one change ships one release note instead of two, and setNextDate is back to the shape a reviewer does not have to re-read.
pieces.context: Three leftovers from PR #15, grouped because none of them is independently worth a plan/implement/review/QA cycle. (1) Balance.tsx:101-103 still parses a preview id by hand — `id.slice(8).split('/')[0]` — while the five sibling call sites (Account.tsx:1562 and the four mobile *AccountTransactions.tsx files) go through `parsePreviewId` from shared/transactions; for a schedule id the two forms are equivalent, so this is consistency, not a defect. (2) upcoming-release-notes/ ships two Bugfixes notes crediting the same author for one user-facing change: `post-scheduled-transaction-on-its-own-date.md` is a leftover from the force-pushed-over revision and describes the advance-based mechanism #15 removes, while `fix-schedule-occurrence-consumption.md` describes the shipped per-occurrence behaviour. (3) app.ts:233-244 kept the `nextDate` → `currentNextDate` rename and the ternary flattening that commit 37cc794 introduced to accommodate a since-deleted param, so a function this PR had no other reason to touch carries ~25 lines of pure re-indentation; restore main's `if (dateCond) { ... }` body and the `nextDate` local name.
acceptance: Balance.tsx reads a preview id's schedule id through parsePreviewId instead of an inline slice-and-split, and its existing test still passes
upcoming-release-notes contains exactly one release note for this fix and it describes the per-occurrence behaviour that shipped, and the release-notes check passes
setNextDate reads as main's if (dateCond) block with the nextDate local name, and the schedules tests pass unchanged
pieces.risk: setNextDate is date arithmetic in the schedule write path. The two forms are semantically identical, so the risk is a bad mechanical revert rather than a design mistake — compare against `git show main:packages/loot-core/src/server/schedules/app.ts` and let the existing schedules tests be the check.
